source.title_on_document: Partnering with Generative AI: Experimental Evaluation of Human-Led and Model-Led Interaction in Human-AI Co-Creation

supplement.where: GitHub repository https://github.com/SM2982/replication-creativity-CHI2026 (p. 5, Section 4; p. 7, Section 4.4; p. 16, Data availability; p. 25, Appendix H). Appendices A-I are part of the paper and are in this PDF (pp. 19-28).
supplement.holds: The repository holds the questionnaire, full measurement details and item wordings, anonymized data, analysis code, and regression diagnostic plots. Every statistic recorded in this form is printed in the PDF: Study 1 arm means, SDs, and Ns (Table 2), hypothesis tests (Tables 3-4), workload contrasts with SEs (Table 10), the within-subject mixed model with SEs and CIs (Tables 12-13), and robustness tests (Tables 14-19). Printed nowhere in the PDF: SEs and the 95 percent CIs that Section 4.5 promises for the main contrasts, and Study 2 arm Ns and arm means and SDs for quality and diversity; these would have to come from the posted data.

paper_design_summary: In Study 1, a preregistered randomized experiment, 502 UK Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of five conditions (GPT-4.1 question-mode, suggestion-mode, model-led one-shot rewriting, vanilla GPT-4.1 chat, or a no-LLM control), 486 were analyzed after preregistered exclusions, and each submitted one idea for repurposing car features (an adapted Alternative Uses Test). Four automotive innovation experts rated each idea's quality (mean of originality and usefulness), and diversity was each idea's cosine distance to the leave-one-out embedding centroid of its condition. Study 2, a preregistered replication with 640 analyzed participants in six conditions (adding a model-led iterative arm; allocation method and platform not stated), used a product-ideation task for UK university students, and 320 student raters recruited on Prolific scored idea quality and purchase intent.

arms.name: Question-mode (Q)
arms.description: Human-led: after an unassisted initial idea, GPT-4.1 shares knowledge or an analogy and asks questions so the participant proposes alternative ideas; the participant picks one and the model asks targeted elaboration questions; the participant refines and submits. Function calls move the dialogue through the phases.

arms.name: Suggestion-mode (S)
arms.description: Human-led: after an unassisted initial idea, GPT-4.1 gives three alternative-idea suggestions (novelty phase) and then three elaboration suggestions (usefulness phase); the participant refines the idea independently.

arms.name: Model-led (M)
arms.description: Participant writes an initial idea (max. 10 words); a one-shot GPT-4.1 prompt rewrites it to raise novelty and usefulness and make it more elaborate (max. 40 words); the participant may refine the model's output before submitting.

arms.name: Vanilla (V)
arms.description: Same chat interface as question-mode with no system prompt or intervention logic; free chat with GPT-4.1, copy and paste allowed.

arms.name: Control (C)
arms.description: Participants generate and refine their idea without any LLM support.

participants.exclusions: Section 4 gives N = 502 for the randomized controlled experiment and says all participants gave informed consent (p. 5). Section 4.1 puts random assignment right after consent (p. 5), and Section 4.3 gives 502 recruited via Prolific (p. 7). n_randomized is therefore 502. The abstract, p. 3, and the Figure 1 caption ('Participants (N = 486) were randomly assigned') give the analyzed count for the randomized experiment instead. Preregistered exclusions then removed 16 assigned participants: failed at least one attention check (10), acknowledged unauthorized AI use during the study (2), nonsense answers (2), participated more than once (1), and did not finish the questionnaire (1). This left 486 analyzed participants. The paper reports no per-arm exclusions and no per-arm counts at assignment. Analyzed arm Ns are from Table 2 (96 + 95 + 101 + 95 + 99 = 486).
participants.who: Prolific participants aged 18 or older, English as first language, approval rate of at least 98 percent, at least 50 previous submissions; final sample aged 18 to 78 (M = 41.34, SD = 12.99); 49.21 percent female, 50.61 percent male, one undisclosed
participants.quote: randomized controlled experiment with N = 502 participants. ... After providing informed consent, participants were randomly assigned to one of the five experimental conditions. ... This resulted in a final sample of N = 486 participants.
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 4 and Section 4.1; p. 7, Section 4.3; p. 12, Table 2; p. 2, Figure 1 caption

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4.1 via the OpenAI API (snapshot gpt-4.1-2025-04-14), temperature 0.7 (p. 6, Section 4.2; p. 19, Table 5 note). The Table 5 Vanilla row reads 'Standard GPT-4 model with default behavior, temperature=0.7, max 500 tokens per response', which conflicts with the note.
ai_tool.how_used: Role differs by arm: vanilla = open_chat (free chat, no system prompt, copy and paste allowed); model-led = refinement (a one-shot prompt rewrites the participant's initial idea of at most 10 words into one idea of at most 40 words, which the participant may refine); suggestion-mode = ideas_supplied (three AI-written alternative ideas, then three elaboration suggestions on the participant's idea; the participant refines independently); question-mode = closest to coach (the AI shares knowledge or an analogy and asks questions, then asks targeted elaboration questions), although Section 4.2 says the LLM generated three alternative ideas. In the model-led and human-led arms the initial idea is written without AI; the scored output is the final idea (pp. 6-7, Section 4.2; p. 19, Appendix A, Table 5).

task.description: Adapted Alternative Uses Test: propose a creative way to repurpose existing car features (steering wheels, brakes, cameras, sensors, screens, lights, speakers) for entirely new uses beyond vehicles; one final idea per participant is scored.
task.duration: Not stated as a time limit; mean total study time 493.33 seconds (SD 418.94) (p. 22, Appendix C, Table 8)

outcomes.name: Idea quality (expert CAT, mean of originality and usefulness)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique: four domain experts (each with at least five months in the innovation department of a major automotive manufacturer) rated every idea on 7-point originality and usefulness scales adapted from Lee and Chung (Appendix D, p. 22); the two ratings were averaged across raters into one quality score; ICC(3,k) = .60 (p. 7, Section 4.4). Separate originality and usefulness results are not reported. Raters judged only the first idea when a person gave several, so there is one scored idea per participant. Linear model with condition as predictor; preregistered one-sided contrasts of estimated marginal means, Holm-adjusted, t(481) (pp. 7-8, Section 4.5). Robustness: Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post hoc tests (p. 25, Table 14). Coded overall_creativity because the score combines originality and usefulness and raters were told it measures creative quality. Unit is output because the paper builds one quality score per idea and the linear model has one row per idea (form-spec field note on unit). Each participant has one scored idea, so the 486 idea rows are the 486 analyzed participants, and the t(481) tests treat each participant as one independent observation.

outcomes.name: Idea diversity (cosine distance to the leave-one-out condition centroid)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Per-idea cosine distance between the idea's OpenAI text-embedding-3-large embedding and the leave-one-out centroid (mean of all other embeddings) in the same condition, following Feuerriegel et al. (p. 7, Section 4.4); higher = more diverse; one idea per participant. The Table 2 note calls it 'within-condition similarity measures', footnote 2 (p. 8) opens 'Semantic similarity was calculated using cosine distance', and Appendix H calls the values 'cosine similarity values', but the text reads higher values as more diverse. Linear model with condition as predictor; preregistered one-sided emmeans contrasts, Holm-adjusted, t(481). Robustness: logit-transformed values and Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn tests (p. 25, Table 15). H2 and H3 compare the human-led modes with model-led and vanilla only; no test against the no-LLM control is reported, but Table 2 gives every arm's mean, SD, and N.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance of each idea's embedding to the leave-one-out centroid (mean of all other embeddings) within its condition; arm means of these per-idea distances are reported
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each output against the centroid of all other outputs in the same condition (leave-one-out), one idea per participant
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Linear model on idea-level scores with condition as predictor; contrasts of estimated marginal means (emmeans) with t(481), Holm-adjusted one-sided p-values, Cohen's d; robustness: logit-transformed values and Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post hoc tests
diversity_detail.notes: One idea per participant, so idea-level and participant-level scores coincide; scores within a condition share one leave-one-out centroid and are not independent. Higher value = more diverse. No test of an AI arm against the no-AI control is reported; the control arm appears only in Table 2.

outcomes.name: Within-subject change in idea diversity (refined, AI-assisted idea vs initial, unassisted idea)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory. Question-mode, suggestion-mode, and model-led arms only (vanilla and control not included): each participant's initial idea (written without AI) and refined idea (after AI interaction) are measured against the centroid of the initial ideas in that condition, called the 'diversity score' (p. 8, Section 5.3 and footnote 2; p. 10, Figure 6). Linear mixed-effects model with participant random intercepts and planned contrasts of estimated marginal means, t(295) (p. 9, Section 5.3; p. 24, Appendix G, Tables 12-13). The paper does not print how many participants or ideas entered this model. Table 2 lists 292 analyzed participants in these three arms. With two ideas each, within-person contrasts would have 289 degrees of freedom, but the paper prints t(295), which fits about 298 participants. The model's sample may therefore differ slightly from the main analysis.

outcomes.name: Elaboration depth of participants' contributions (coded Levels 1-5)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory. Two trained raters (domain expertise not described) independently coded a randomly selected subset of 20 conversations per condition (80 ideas) on a five-level ordinal scale from Level 1 (LLM-led echo, pure acceptance) to Level 5 (human-led reframing); weighted kappa = 0.628; consensus scores used (p. 9, Section 5.4). The scheme adapts Guilford's elaboration construct; a level depends on which elements the participant added and whether the AI or the participant supplied them (p. 7, Section 4.4; p. 23, Appendix E, Table 9). It therefore measures the participant's contribution beyond the LLM input in the refinement turns, not the detail or creativity of the final idea. The statistics are descriptive: level percentages in the text for three arms and arm means only in Figure 7. No control arm can be coded.

contrasts.reported: Descriptive only, no test. Twenty randomly selected conversations were coded per AI arm (80 ideas). Model-led: 90% of participants accepted the model refinement without further elaboration. Suggestion-mode: 25% did not elaborate at all and 55% made minor elaboration. Question-mode: 60% elaborated substantially and 40% added an incrementally new idea. Figure 7 plots mean elaboration depth (levels 1-5 rescaled to 1-7) for all four AI arms, including vanilla, with no numbers printed. The paper also correlated elaboration depth with its dependent variables: idea diversity r = 0.28, p = .032; quality and ownership both p > .15. The number of coded ideas in these correlations is not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5.4; p. 10, Section 5.4 (correlations); p. 11, Figure 7; p. 23, Table 9

outcomes.name: Purchase intent (intention-to-buy rating by student raters)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory. A single intention-to-buy item was added to the rating instrument following Girotra et al. and rated by the 320 student raters on a 1-7 scale (p. 11, Section 6.1; Figure 8 caption, p. 27). It captures perceived market viability. Means and SDs are printed in the text (p. 13) and 95 percent CIs only in Figure 8. No arm Ns and no tests are printed. Which model-led arm received 2.50 and which 2.24 is unresolved (see open_questions).

eligibility.reason: Study 1 meets all three criteria. Individual participants were randomly assigned to four GPT-4.1 conditions or a no-LLM control (p. 5, Section 4.1). Of 502 randomized, 486 were analyzed after preregistered exclusions, 95 to 101 per arm (p. 5, Section 4; p. 7, Section 4.3; p. 12, Table 2), far above 50. The outcomes are expert ratings and embedding diversity of each submitted idea, which AI-arm participants wrote with the GPT-4.1 output available (pp. 5-7, Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.4). Study 2 (640 analyzed, p. 11) is described as a preregistered replication in six conditions, but the paper does not state random assignment, platform, or arm sizes for it. Study 2 is therefore coded design_class other with criterion 1 unclear, and its records need the preregistration (aspredicted.org/de6md8) or the authors before they enter pooled estimates. The paper's core status rests on Study 1 and does not depend on Study 2.

one_line_finding: In Study 1 (486 analyzed), expert-rated idea quality rose over the no-AI control with model-led rewriting (3.11 vs 2.68, t(481) = 3.86, d = 0.55) and question-mode (2.96, t(481) = 2.49, d = 0.36) but not with vanilla GPT-4.1 chat (2.70, d = 0.02) or suggestion-mode (2.78, d = 0.13), and question-mode ideas were more diverse than model-led ideas (0.379 vs 0.309, d = 0.76; no AI-versus-control diversity test) (p. 12, Tables 2-3).
open_questions: Study 2 does not state random assignment, recruitment platform, country, inclusion criteria, exclusions, or arm sizes (pp. 10-11, Section 6.1). The paper calls it a second, preregistered experiment and a replication (p. 3; p. 10, Section 6.1), so the final form codes its design_class other (not online_rct) and its criterion 1 unclear. Confirm allocation from the preregistration (https://aspredicted.org/de6md8.pdf) or the authors before Study 2 records enter pooled estimates.

Study 2 purchase intent: Section 6.3 (p. 13) gives model-led iterative M = 2.50 and one-shot M = 2.24, but Section 7.1 (p. 14) says the one-shot condition had descriptively higher purchase intent, and Figure 8 (p. 27) plots about 2.50 under 'Model-Led', the label Figure 9 (p. 28) uses for the one-shot arm (its caption gives the one-shot workload 44.04 and AI attribution 39.98). 'Generation-Mode' is never defined, and the Figure 8 caption says five conditions while six are plotted. The posted data or the authors would settle which arm received 2.50.

Study 2 analysis: Section 6.2 says linear mixed-effects models for quality and simple linear regressions for diversity; the Table 4 caption says the quality z-statistics come from an ordinal mixed model; Table 17 reports a cumulative link mixed model with slightly different z (5.55 vs 5.59 for H1a); the Table 18 note calls the diversity parametric test a linear mixed model.

Diversity labels: the Table 2 note calls idea diversity 'within-condition similarity measures', footnote 2 opens 'Semantic similarity was calculated using cosine distance', and Appendix H speaks of 'cosine similarity values', but Section 4.4 defines a cosine distance and the text reads higher values as more diverse, which matches the signs of the hypothesis tests. The posted data could confirm the sign convention.

Text vs table mismatches in Study 1: H2b p = .983 (p. 8) vs .984 (Table 3); H3a d = 0.29 (p. 8) vs 0.27 (Table 3); suggestion-mode within-subject t(295) = -2.67 (p. 9) vs t = -2.78 (Table 13); question-mode change t = 7.24 and CI [0.049, 0.085] in Table 12 vs 7.20 and [0.049, 0.086] in Table 13.

Study 1 counts and procedure: n_randomized is coded 502 from Section 4 ('randomized controlled experiment with N = 502 participants', p. 5), with assignment after consent (p. 5, Section 4.1) and all 16 exclusions among assigned participants (p. 7, Section 4.3). The abstract, p. 3, and the Figure 1 caption give N = 486 for the randomized experiment, and per-arm counts at assignment are not printed. The Figure 1 caption also says all participants were instructed to refine their idea using the LLM, which cannot apply to the no-LLM control (p. 5, Section 4.1; p. 7, Section 4.2).

No AI-versus-control test of diversity is reported in either study; Study 1 Table 2 gives every arm's mean, SD, and N (control 0.343, SD 0.108), and Study 2 prints no diversity arm means. Output-level diversity scores share a leave-one-out condition centroid, so they are not independent within a condition.

Question-mode description: Section 4.2 (p. 6) says the LLM generated three alternative ideas, while the Table 5 prompt (p. 19) and the Figure 2 caption (p. 6) have the LLM share knowledge or an analogy and ask the participant to propose alternatives; this bears on the AI-role code (coach vs ideas_supplied).
Table 5 (p. 19) labels the vanilla model 'Standard GPT-4 model' while its note and Section 4.2 say all AI conditions used GPT-4.1.
The Cohen's d standardizer is not stated; Section 4.5 says each estimate is reported with its 95 percent CI, but Tables 3 and 4 print no CIs and no standard errors for the main contrasts.

S1-O3 sample: the paper does not print how many participants entered the within-subject mixed model. Table 2 lists 292 analyzed participants in the question-mode, suggestion-mode, and model-led arms. With two ideas each, within-person contrasts would have 289 degrees of freedom, but the paper prints t(295) (p. 9, Section 5.3), which fits about 298 participants. The posted data would show the model's sample.

S1-O4 correlations: the paper does not say how many coded ideas entered the correlation of elaboration depth with idea diversity (r = 0.28, p = .032, p. 10, Section 5.4). With all 80 coded ideas, r = 0.28 would give a two-sided p near .012, and p = .032 fits about 60 ideas. The posted data would settle it.

S2-O3 unit: the paper does not say whether the purchase-intent means, SDs, and CIs are computed over single ratings or over idea means. The printed SDs (0.49 to 0.62 on a 1-7 item) and the Figure 8 interval half-widths (0.089 to 0.123) fit idea means, so the form codes unit output. The posted data or code would confirm it.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reported rather than scored on the output: perceived idea ownership (preregistered H4-H5; Tables 2-4, 16, 19), perceived cognitive workload (Tables 2, 10, 11; Figures 4 and 9), creative self-efficacy (Table 2; Figure 7), the UTAUT user-experience scales (Figure 7), and the Study 2 self-vs-AI attribution item (Figure 9). S1-O4 (elaboration depth) is listed although it codes participants' contributions in the conversation rather than the final idea; it is descriptive only. In the model-led and human-led arms of Study 1 participants wrote an initial idea without AI, interacted with GPT-4.1, and submitted a final idea, which is the scored output; vanilla participants chatted freely with GPT-4.1. Each participant submitted one scored idea, so S1-O1 and S1-O2 have one row per idea, which is also one row per participant (unit output, n_units 486). Under codebook rule 3 the primary with_ai record for Study 1 is vanilla vs control (H1d, d = 0.02, Table 3); for across_people no vanilla-vs-control diversity test exists, only the Table 2 means (0.378 vs 0.343). Table 3 and Table 4 p-values are Holm-adjusted and one-sided (Section 4.5; Table 4 caption). The power analysis required about 78 per group and 100 per group was the preregistered target (p. 7); a 50-person pilot tested the system and is not analyzed (p. 7). Studies 1 and 2 are separate samples (486 and 640 analyzed, the paper's total N = 1,126, p. 3). Table 8 (p. 22) gives pooled Study 1 correlations, including idea quality with diversity r = -.26. The Data availability statement is on p. 16 (both raw forms said p. 15). Study 2 is coded design_class other because the paper never states how its 640 participants were allocated or where they were recruited. Its contrasts keep the comparison types ai_vs_bau and ai_design because those codes name the arms compared, while design_class, assignment.randomized, and criterion 1 carry the missing allocation. If the preregistration confirms random assignment on an online panel, Study 2 becomes online_rct. This form replaces an earlier reconciliation dated 4 October 2026 that was built from an earlier pair of raw forms.

open_items.item: Study 2 purchase-intent arm attribution (open question 2, also the one unresolved reconciliation difference): Section 6.3 gives the iterative arm 2.50 and the one-shot arm 2.24, but Section 7.1 and the Figure 8 and Figure 9 labels point the other way. Secondary outcome only.
Study 2 analysis models (open question 3): Section 6.2, the Table 4 caption, and the Table 17 and Table 18 notes name different models for quality and diversity.
Diversity labels (open question 4): the Table 2 note, footnote 2, and Appendix H say similarity, while Section 4.4 defines a cosine distance; the test signs fit distance.
Study 1 text versus table mismatches (open question 5): H2b p, H3a d, the suggestion-mode within-subject t, and the question-mode change in Table 12 versus Table 13. The form records both values.

Study 1 count at assignment and the Figure 1 caption (open question 6): the form codes 502 randomized from Section 4, while the abstract, p. 3, and Figure 1 say N = 486; per-arm counts at assignment are not printed. Both counts are far above 50.

No AI-versus-control diversity test in either study (open question 7); Study 1 Table 2 gives every arm's mean, SD, and N, Study 2 prints no diversity arm means, and output-level scores share a leave-one-out centroid.

Question-mode description (open question 8): Section 4.2 says the LLM generated three alternative ideas, while the Table 5 prompt and Figure 2 have the participant propose them. It bears only on the per-arm AI-role code.
Table 5 labels the vanilla model 'Standard GPT-4' while its note and Section 4.2 say GPT-4.1 for all AI arms (open question 9).
Cohen's d standardizer is not stated. Tables 3 and 4 print no SEs or 95 percent CIs for the main contrasts, although Section 4.5 promises the 95 percent CIs (open question 10).
S1-O3 sample (open question 11): t(295) fits about 298 participants, not the 292 analyzed in the three arms.
S1-O4 correlation sample (open question 12): r = 0.28 with p = .032 fits about 60 coded ideas, not 80.
S2-O3 unit (open question 13): coded output from the printed SDs and the Figure 8 intervals; the paper does not state it.
